about: Sourced life stories for prophets and people of the exile: Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Job, John the Baptist, Mordecai and Haman. Written from the KJV text of Scripture; there is no reviewed dossier for these people.

elijah-1ki-17-1.short: Elijah the Tishbite, of Gilead, a prophet in Ahab's days, answered by fire on mount Carmel and taken up into heaven by a whirlwind.

paragraphs.text: Kings names no father or family for Elijah; it calls him "Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead". He told King Ahab that there would be no dew nor rain "but according to my word". The LORD sent him to hide by the brook Cherith, where ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening, until the brook dried up.

He was sent on to Zarephath, which belonged to Zidon, where a widow gathering sticks had only a handful of meal and a little oil. He asked her to make him a little cake first, and her barrel of meal did not waste nor her cruse of oil fail. When her son fell sick until "there was no breath left in him", Elijah carried him up to the loft, stretched himself on the child three times and cried to the LORD, and the child revived. The woman said, "Now by this I know that thou art a man of God". In Luke, Jesus says that of the many widows in Israel in the days of Elias, he was sent to none but "a woman that was a widow" in Sarepta, a city of Sidon.

In the third year the LORD sent him back to Ahab, who greeted him, "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" Elijah answered that Ahab and his father's house had troubled Israel by following Baalim, and had all Israel and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal gathered to mount Carmel. There he asked the people, "How long halt ye between two opinions?" Baal's prophets called on their god from morning until past midday with no answer, while Elijah mocked them. Then he repaired the altar of the LORD with twelve stones, had water poured on the offering three times and prayed; "the fire of the LORD fell", and at his word the people took the prophets of Baal, and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slew them there.

On the top of Carmel he cast himself down with his face between his knees and sent his servant seven times to look toward the sea, until a little cloud rose "like a man's hand"; a great rain followed, and Elijah ran before Ahab to Jezreel. When Jezebel swore to take his life, he fled to Beer-sheba and went a day's journey into the wilderness, where he sat under a juniper tree and asked to die: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life". An angel twice woke him to eat, and he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the mount of God.

In a cave at Horeb the word of the LORD asked him, "What doest thou here, Elijah?", and he answered that the prophets had been slain and "I, even I only, am left". A wind, an earthquake and a fire passed, but the LORD was not in them; after the fire came "a still small voice". The LORD sent him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha as prophet in his place, and told him of seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal; Paul recalls this answer in Romans. Elijah found Elisha plowing and cast his mantle upon him.

After Ahab had taken Naboth's vineyard, Elijah met him there with the LORD's word against his house, and Ahab said, "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" When Ahab humbled himself, the LORD told Elijah that the evil would come in his son's days. When King Ahaziah sent to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, Elijah turned his messengers back with word that he would die; they described "an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins". Fire from heaven consumed two captains sent with their fifties to fetch him, and he went down with the third, and Ahaziah died as Elijah had said. Chronicles adds that a writing came from Elijah the prophet to Jehoram king of Judah.

When the LORD was about to take him up, Elijah went from Gilgal to Beth-el, to Jericho and to the Jordan, and each time Elisha would not leave him. Elijah struck the waters with his mantle and the two crossed on dry ground, and Elisha asked for "a double portion of thy spirit". As they walked and talked, a chariot of fire and horses of fire parted them, "and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven". Fifty men searched for him three days and did not find him.

Malachi says that God will send "Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD". In Luke the angel says that John would go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias", and in Matthew Jesus says of John, "this is Elias, which was for to come"; in John's Gospel, John himself, asked "Art thou Elias?", answers, "I am not." Matthew, Mark and Luke tell that Elias appeared with Moses, talking with Jesus on the mountain. James writes that Elias "was a man subject to like passions as we are", who prayed that it might not rain, and prayed again for rain.

elisha-1ki-19-16.short: Son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, called from his plough when Elijah cast his mantle on him, and after Elijah was taken up, a prophet in Israel.

paragraphs.text: Elisha was the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah. At Horeb the LORD told Elijah to anoint him to be prophet "in thy room", and Elijah found him plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle upon him. Elisha asked leave to kiss his father and his mother; then he slew a yoke of oxen, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, gave it to the people, and went after Elijah and "ministered unto him". Later a servant of the king of Israel described him as the man "which poured water on the hands of Elijah".

On the day Elijah was taken up, Elisha three times refused to leave him, and asked for "a double portion of thy spirit". He saw Elijah go and cried, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof"; then he took up Elijah's mantle, struck the Jordan, and crossed, and the sons of the prophets said, "The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha." At Jericho he healed the spring with salt, and on the way to Beth-el, when children mocked him, "Go up, thou bald head", he cursed them in the name of the LORD and two she bears tore forty and two of them. When the kings of Israel, Judah and Edom had no water in their war with Moab, he told them the valley would be filled with water, and in the morning it was.

A widow of one of the sons of the prophets, whose two sons a creditor was coming to take as bondmen, had nothing but a pot of oil; at Elisha's word she poured it into borrowed vessels until there was not a vessel more, and sold it to pay her debt. A woman of Shunem made a little chamber for him on her wall, and he told her she would have a son, and she did. When the child died, she laid him on the prophet's bed and rode to Elisha at mount Carmel; Elisha came, prayed and lay upon the child, and "the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes." At Gilgal, when the sons of the prophets cried, "there is death in the pot", he cast meal in and there was no harm in it, and twenty barley loaves fed a hundred men with some left.

Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a leper, and a captive maid from Israel told her mistress that the prophet in Samaria would recover him. Elisha sent word to wash in Jordan seven times; Naaman went away in a rage, then went down and dipped himself, and "he was clean". Elisha refused his gifts, but his servant Gehazi ran after Naaman, took silver and garments, and denied it to his master, and he went out "a leper as white as snow". In Luke, Jesus says that of the many lepers in Israel in the time of Eliseus, only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed.

When the king of Syria learned that Elisha was telling the king of Israel where Syria would camp, he sent horses, chariots and a great host by night to take him at Dothan. Elisha prayed that his servant's eyes be opened, and the young man saw that "the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha". He prayed that the Syrians be struck with blindness, led them into Samaria, and told the king not to smite them but to feed them and send them home. Later, in the siege of Samaria, the king swore to take Elisha's head, and Elisha said that by the next day fine flour would sell for a shekel in the gate; it came to pass as he had said.

At Damascus, when the sick Ben-hadad sent Hazael to ask whether he would recover, Elisha wept and told him, "The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria." He sent one of the children of the prophets to anoint Jehu king over Israel. When Elisha fell sick of the sickness he died of, King Joash came and wept over him with the words Elisha had cried after Elijah, "O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof"; Elisha had him shoot an arrow from the east window and strike the ground, and was angry that he struck only three times. Elisha died and was buried, and when a dead man was cast into his sepulchre and touched his bones, the man revived and stood up on his feet.

isaiah-2ki-19-2.short: Isaiah son of Amoz, a prophet in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, who carried the LORD's word to Ahaz and to Hezekiah.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah was the son of Amoz, and his book opens as his vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. In the year that King Uzziah died he saw "the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up", with seraphims crying, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". He said, "Woe is me! for I am undone"; a seraph laid a live coal from the altar on his mouth, and when the Lord asked, "Whom shall I send", Isaiah answered, "Here am I; send me." Chronicles says that Isaiah the prophet wrote the acts of Uzziah.

When Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel came up against Jerusalem, the LORD sent Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub to meet King Ahaz at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, and to tell him, "Take heed, and be quiet; fear not". The LORD spoke again to Ahaz, bidding him ask a sign; when Ahaz said, "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD", the answer came: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." A son born to Isaiah by "the prophetess" was named at the LORD's word Maher-shalal-hash-baz, and Isaiah said, "I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel".

In the year that Tartan, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, took Ashdod, the LORD told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoe, "And he did so, walking naked and barefoot." The LORD said that his servant Isaiah had walked so three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia.

King Hezekiah sent Eliakim, Shebna the scribe and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah: the king of Assyria had sent Rab-shakeh "to reproach the living God", and they asked Isaiah to pray for the remnant. Isaiah sent back, "Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard", and later sent Hezekiah word that his prayer against Sennacherib had been heard. Kings says that that night the angel of the LORD smote the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib went home to Nineveh. Chronicles says that Hezekiah the king and the prophet Isaiah "prayed and cried to heaven".

When Hezekiah was sick unto death, Isaiah came and told him, "Set thine house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live." Kings tells that before Isaiah had gone out into the middle court the word of the LORD sent him back: the king's prayer was heard, and fifteen years would be added to his days. Isaiah had a lump of figs laid on the boil, and when Hezekiah asked for a sign, Isaiah let him choose whether the shadow should go forward or back ten degrees; Hezekiah chose back, Isaiah cried to the LORD, and it went back on the dial of Ahaz. In the book of Isaiah the LORD gives the sign of the shadow without offering a choice, and the figs are told at the end of the chapter.

When envoys came from Berodach-baladan king of Babylon (Isaiah's book calls him Merodach-baladan) and Hezekiah showed them all his treasures, Isaiah asked him, "What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee?", and told him that all in his house would be carried to Babylon. Chronicles says the rest of Hezekiah's acts are written in "the vision of Isaiah the prophet". Scripture does not tell how Isaiah's life ended. In Luke, Jesus reads in the synagogue at Nazareth from "the book of the prophet Esaias", and John's Gospel says, "These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory".

jeremiah-2ch-35-25.short: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, of the priests of Anathoth, a prophet from Josiah's days until Jerusalem fell, beaten, imprisoned and cast into a dungeon for his words.

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, "of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin". The word of the LORD came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, and on through Jehoiakim's reign to the carrying away of Jerusalem in Zedekiah's eleventh year. The LORD told him, "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee", and when Jeremiah said, "I cannot speak: for I am a child", the LORD touched his mouth: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth." Chronicles says that Jeremiah lamented for Josiah.

The men of Anathoth told him, "Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand", and the LORD told him not to take a wife or have sons or daughters "in this place". He was sent to the potter's house, where he watched a marred vessel made again into another and heard, "as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand". He was sent to break a potter's earthen bottle in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and when he came back from Tophet and spoke in the court of the LORD's house, Pashur the son of Immer, chief governor in the house of the LORD, smote him and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin. Let out the next day, Jeremiah told him that the LORD had called his name not Pashur but "Magor-missabib".

Early in Jehoiakim's reign, when he said in the court of the LORD's house that it would be made like Shiloh, the priests, the prophets and the people took him, saying, "Thou shalt surely die"; the princes and some elders spoke for him, and "the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah". The LORD told him to make bonds and yokes and put them on his neck, and he told King Zedekiah, "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon". The prophet Hananiah took the yoke from his neck and broke it; Jeremiah told him the LORD had not sent him and that he would die that year, and Hananiah died in the seventh month. Jeremiah also sent a letter to the captives in Babylon: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens".

In Jehoiakim's fourth year the LORD told him to write all his words in a roll, and Baruch the son of Neriah wrote them from his mouth; Jeremiah said, "I am shut up; I cannot go into the house of the LORD", and sent Baruch to read them there on a fast day. The princes who heard it told Baruch, "Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah". When the roll was read to King Jehoiakim by the fire in his winterhouse, it was cut with a penknife three or four leaves at a time and cast into the fire until it was all burned, and the king commanded that Baruch and Jeremiah be taken, "but the LORD hid them." Jeremiah gave Baruch another roll and dictated it again, "and there were added besides unto them many like words."

Under Zedekiah, while the Chaldeans' army had drawn back for fear of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out for the land of Benjamin and was seized in the gate of Benjamin by Irijah, who said, "Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans"; the princes smote him and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe. Zedekiah had him brought out and asked him secretly, "Is there any word from the LORD?", and Jeremiah answered that the king would be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. The king moved him to the court of the prison, with a piece of bread daily from the bakers' street. There, with the city besieged, he bought his uncle's son Hanameel's field at Anathoth for seventeen shekels of silver and gave the deeds to Baruch to keep in an earthen vessel.

When princes heard him tell the people that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live, they asked the king to put him to death, and Zedekiah said, "he is in your hand". They let him down with cords into the dungeon of Malchiah, where there was no water but mire, "so Jeremiah sunk in the mire." Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch in the king's house, spoke to the king, and with thirty men drew Jeremiah up with cords, with old rags under his armholes. Jeremiah stayed in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken, and a word of the LORD promised Ebed-melech that he would be delivered, "because thou hast put thy trust in me".

When the city was taken, Nebuchadrezzar charged the captain of his guard concerning Jeremiah, "look well to him". Chapter 39 says he was taken out of the court of the prison and committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam; chapter 40 says the captain of the guard loosed him from chains at Ramah among the captives and let him go where he would, and he went to Gedaliah at Mizpah. After Gedaliah was killed, Johanan and the captains refused the word Jeremiah brought them, "Go ye not into Egypt", and took the remnant, with "Jeremiah the prophet, and Baruch the son of Neriah", to Tahpanhes in Egypt. In Egypt he still spoke the word of the LORD to the Jews there, who told him, "we will not hearken unto thee"; Scripture does not say how or where he died.

His book closes, after the words "Thus far are the words of Jeremiah", with an account of the city's fall like that in 2 Kings 25, with differences: Jeremiah 52 has the captain of the guard come to Jerusalem on the tenth day of the fifth month where Kings has the seventh, and adds the numbers that Nebuchadrezzar carried away. Chronicles says that the seventy years the land lay desolate fulfilled "the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah", and Chronicles and Ezra both say that the LORD stirred up Cyrus to make his proclamation so that this word might be fulfilled; and Daniel says he understood the number of the years from the word that came to Jeremiah the prophet. Matthew twice cites "Jeremy the prophet".

daniel-ezk-14-14.short: A young man of Judah taken to Babylon and named Belteshazzar, who told Nebuchadnezzar his dream, read the writing on the wall, and was kept from the lions.

paragraphs.text: This record begins in Ezekiel, where the LORD twice names "Noah, Daniel, and Job" as men who by their righteousness would deliver only their own souls, and tells the prince of Tyrus, "thou art wiser than Daniel". Ezekiel does not say whether this is the Daniel whose life the book of Daniel tells.

The book of Daniel tells that after Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem in the third year of Jehoiakim, he had young men brought "of the king's seed, and of the princes", to be taught the learning and tongue of the Chaldeans. Among them, of the children of Judah, were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, and the prince of the eunuchs named Daniel Belteshazzar. Daniel would not defile himself with the king's meat and wine, and asked for ten days of pulse and water; at the end of them the four looked fairer than all the rest. God gave the four knowledge and skill, "and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams", and the king found them ten times better than all his magicians and astrologers.

When Nebuchadnezzar demanded that his wise men tell him his dream as well as its meaning, and ordered them all slain when they could not, Daniel asked for time and asked his three companions to seek mercy of the God of heaven. The secret was revealed to Daniel in a night vision, and he blessed God. Before the king he said that no wise man could show it, "But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets", and told him the dream, a great image of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay. The king fell on his face before Daniel, made him ruler over the province of Babylon and chief of the governors over the wise men, and at his request set Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego over the province's affairs.

Nebuchadnezzar tells in his own words how Daniel, "whose name was Belteshazzar", came in before him and heard his dream of a great tree; Daniel was astonied for an hour, and counselled the king to "break off thy sins by righteousness". Under King Belshazzar, when the fingers of a man's hand wrote on the palace wall during a feast at which they drank from the vessels taken out of the temple in Jerusalem, the queen told the king of Daniel. Daniel told him to keep his gifts, read the writing, "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN", and gave its meaning; he was clothed in scarlet and proclaimed third ruler in the kingdom. That night Belshazzar was slain, and Darius the Median took the kingdom.

Darius set Daniel first of three presidents over the kingdom, and thought to set him over the whole realm. The other presidents and princes, finding no fault in him except "concerning the law of his God", had the king sign a decree that for thirty days no one should ask a petition of any God or man save of the king. Daniel went home and, with his windows open toward Jerusalem, kneeled three times a day and prayed, "as he did aforetime". He was cast into the den of lions, and in the morning he told the king, "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths"; his accusers were cast in instead, and Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and of Cyrus the Persian.

In the first year of Belshazzar Daniel dreamed of four great beasts coming up from the sea, and in the third year he saw in a vision, by the river Ulai, a ram with two horns; Gabriel was sent to make him understand it, and afterward Daniel fainted and was sick certain days. In the first year of Darius he understood by books the number of the years "whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet", seventy years, and set his face to seek God with fasting, sackcloth and ashes; Gabriel came to him while he prayed. In the third year of Cyrus, after mourning three full weeks, he saw by the river Hiddekel a man clothed in linen; then a hand touched him, and he was called "a man greatly beloved".

The book closes with Daniel told to "shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end". When he asked what the end of these things would be, he heard, "Go thy way, Daniel", and that he would rest and stand in his lot "at the end of the days". The book says Daniel continued "even unto the first year of king Cyrus", and dates his last vision in the third year of Cyrus; it does not say how he died. In Matthew and Mark, Jesus speaks of "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet".

job-job-1-1.short: A man of Uz whom God called perfect and upright, who lost his children, goods and health, spoke with his friends and with God, and was restored.

paragraphs.text: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." He had seven sons and three daughters and great flocks and herds, "so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east". When his children had feasted, he rose early and offered burnt offerings for each of them, saying, "It may be that my sons have sinned".

The book tells of a day when the sons of God came before the LORD and Satan came among them; the LORD asked, "Hast thou considered my servant Job", and Satan answered, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" In one day messengers told Job that his oxen, asses, sheep and camels were taken or burned with the servants, and that a great wind had struck the house where his sons and daughters were eating, "and they are dead". Job rent his mantle, shaved his head, fell down and worshipped: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." The book says, "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly."

Satan came again, and the LORD gave Job into his hand, "but save his life"; Job was struck with sore boils from the sole of his foot to his crown, and sat among the ashes scraping himself with a potsherd. His wife said, "curse God, and die", and he answered, "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" His three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite, came to mourn with him and comfort him, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word.

Then Job opened his mouth and cursed his day. The book gives the speeches of Job and his friends in turn, until "The words of Job are ended." A younger man, Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, then spoke, angry with Job and with the three friends. At last the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, asking, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?", and Job answered, "I will lay mine hand upon my mouth."

Job said to the LORD, "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." The LORD told Eliphaz that he and his two friends had not spoken of him "the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath", and sent them to offer burnt offerings and have Job pray for them. When Job prayed for his friends, the LORD gave him twice as much as he had before; he had again seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, and gave the daughters an inheritance among their brothers. He lived a hundred and forty years after this and saw four generations, and died "old and full of days".
Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as men whose righteousness would deliver only their own souls. James writes, "Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord".

john-mat-3-1.short: John, son of the priest Zacharias and Elisabeth, who preached repentance and baptized by the Jordan, baptized Jesus, and was beheaded by Herod the tetrarch.

paragraphs.text: Luke tells that John's father Zacharias was a priest of the course of Abia and his mother Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron; they had no child, and both were old. While Zacharias burned incense in the temple, the angel Gabriel told him his wife would bear a son to be called John, who would "drink neither wine nor strong drink" and would go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias"; Zacharias doubted and was struck dumb. When Mary, whom the angel calls Elisabeth's cousin, came to the house, the babe leaped in Elisabeth's womb. At his circumcision they would have called him Zacharias, but his mother said, "he shall be called John", and his father wrote, "His name is John", and his mouth was opened. The child grew, "and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel."

Luke says that the word of God came to "John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness" in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and he preached "the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins". Matthew and Mark describe him clothed in camel's hair with a leather girdle, eating locusts and wild honey, and say that Jerusalem and Judaea went out to him (Matthew adds "all the region round about Jordan") and were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins. Matthew and Luke apply to him the words of Esaias, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness", and in John's Gospel he says them of himself. In Luke he called the multitude that came to be baptized a "generation of vipers", where Matthew has him say it to the Pharisees and Sadducees, and Luke adds that he told the people to share coats and food, the publicans to exact no more than was appointed, and the soldiers to do violence to no man.

He told the people that one mightier than he was coming after him, who would baptize with the Holy Ghost. Matthew tells that when Jesus came to Jordan to be baptized, John forbade him, "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?", until Jesus said, "Suffer it to be so now"; Mark says that Jesus "was baptized of John in Jordan", and Luke tells the baptism without naming John at that point. In John's Gospel, when priests and Levites came to ask who he was, he said, "I am not the Christ", and that he was not Elias; the next day he said of Jesus, "Behold the Lamb of God", and when he said it again the day after, two of his disciples, one of them Andrew, followed Jesus.

John's Gospel says he went on baptizing at Aenon near to Salim, and when his disciples told him that all men were coming to Jesus, he answered, "He must increase, but I must decrease." Matthew, Mark and Luke tell that Herod the tetrarch put John in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife; in Matthew John had told him, "It is not lawful for thee to have her", and Luke adds that John reproved him "for all the evils which Herod had done". Matthew and Luke tell that John sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus, "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?" (Matthew says John was then in prison), and Jesus told them to tell John what they saw and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised.

Matthew and Luke record Jesus asking the crowds what they had gone into the wilderness to see, "A reed shaken with the wind?", and calling John a prophet "and more than a prophet"; among those born of women none is greater than John, he says, yet, in Matthew's words, "he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." In Matthew, Jesus also says, "this is Elias, which was for to come", and after the transfiguration the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptist. He says that John came "neither eating nor drinking" and people said, "He hath a devil"; in John's Gospel Jesus calls him "a burning and a shining light".

Matthew and Mark tell that at Herod's birthday the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked; at her mother's word she asked for "John Baptist's head in a charger", and Herod, though sorry, for his oath's sake had John beheaded in the prison. Mark adds that Herodias "had a quarrel against him", and that Herod "feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy". His disciples took up the body and buried it, and Matthew says they went and told Jesus; Luke tells it only in Herod's words, "John have I beheaded". In Acts, Paul finds disciples at Ephesus baptized "Unto John's baptism" and tells them, "John verily baptized with the baptism of repentance", saying that the people should believe on him who came after him.

mordecai-est-2-5.short: A Benjamite Jew in Shushan who raised his orphaned cousin Esther, would not bow to Haman, and rose to be next to King Ahasuerus.

paragraphs.text: Mordecai was "a certain Jew" in Shushan the palace, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, "a Benjamite"; the next verse ties his line to the captives carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah king of Judah. He brought up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle Abihail, and when her father and mother died he took her for his own daughter. When she was taken into the king's house, he charged her not to show her people or her kindred, and walked every day before the court of the women's house to know how she did.

As he sat in the king's gate, Mordecai learned that two of the king's chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, sought to lay hand on King Ahasuerus; he told Esther, she told the king in Mordecai's name, and the two were hanged, and it was written in the book of the chronicles. When the king promoted Haman the Agagite and commanded all in the gate to bow to him, "Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence"; he had told the king's servants that he was a Jew, and they told Haman. Haman, full of wrath, sought to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom, "even the people of Mordecai".

When the decree to destroy the Jews went out, Mordecai rent his clothes, put on sackcloth with ashes and cried in the midst of the city. He sent Esther a copy of the decree and charged her to go in to the king for her people; when she answered that whoever came in to the king uncalled was put to death unless the king held out the golden sceptre, he sent back, "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" At her word he gathered the Jews of Shushan to fast for her three days.

At the word of his wife and friends, Haman had a gallows made fifty cubits high to hang Mordecai on. That night the king could not sleep, heard read from the chronicles how Mordecai had told of the two chamberlains, and learned that nothing had been done for him; and Haman himself had to array Mordecai in royal apparel and bring him on horseback through the city, proclaiming, "Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour." When Esther named Haman as the enemy, he was hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai; the king gave Mordecai the ring he had taken from Haman, and Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.

Letters were written in the king's name as Mordecai commanded, granting the Jews in every city to stand for their life, and Mordecai went out from the king in royal apparel of blue and white with a great crown of gold, and Shushan rejoiced. The rulers of the provinces helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai fell on them, "for this man Mordecai waxed greater and greater". He wrote to the Jews in all the provinces to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year, the days of Purim, and Esther the queen and Mordecai wrote again to confirm them. The book ends with Mordecai "next unto king Ahasuerus", "seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed."

haman-est-3-1.short: Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, set above all the princes of Ahasuerus, who plotted to destroy the Jews and was hanged on the gallows he made for Mordecai.

paragraphs.text: Haman was the son of Hammedatha the Agagite. King Ahasuerus promoted him, set his seat above all the princes with him, and commanded the servants in the king's gate to bow to him. When Mordecai would not bow, Haman was "full of wrath", and thinking scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone, he sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom.

They cast Pur, that is the lot, before Haman from month to month, to the twelfth month, Adar. Haman told the king of "a certain people scattered abroad" whose laws were diverse and who did not keep the king's laws, and offered ten thousand talents of silver for their destruction; the king gave him his ring. Letters went out in the king's name to destroy all Jews, young and old, little children and women, on the thirteenth day of Adar, "And the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed."

Esther invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and Haman went out "joyful and with a glad heart" until he saw Mordecai in the gate, who did not stand up for him. At home he told Zeresh his wife and his friends of his riches, his many children and his promotion: "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate"; they told him to have a gallows made fifty cubits high, and he did. Coming to the king to ask that Mordecai be hanged, he was asked what should be done to "the man whom the king delighteth to honour"; thinking it was himself, he named royal apparel, a horse and a crown, and was told to do all of it for Mordecai.

He hasted home mourning with his head covered, and his wise men and Zeresh told him that if Mordecai was of the seed of the Jews, "thou shalt not prevail against him". At Esther's second banquet she asked the king for her life and her people's, and named "this wicked Haman" as the enemy. When the king went out in his wrath, Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther and fell on the bed where she was; the chamberlain Harbonah told of the gallows Haman had made for Mordecai, and Haman was hanged on it.

The king gave the house of Haman to Esther, and the ring he had taken from Haman to Mordecai. Esther asked the king to reverse "the letters devised by Haman", and new letters were written granting the Jews to stand for their life. On the thirteenth of Adar Haman's ten sons, whom the book names, were slain in Shushan, and at Esther's request they were hanged. The book calls Haman "the enemy of all the Jews", who had cast Pur, and the days of Purim are named after it.
